blocks.text: Eleanor telephoned Billy’s office that evening. He had just set his notebook beside the lamp when he heard her voice.
“William. Bring your questions here tomorrow morning. I would rather not have another conversation on the City Hall steps.”
Billy looked at the space where the invoice had been. “I’ll bring my notebook.”

At the Blackwells’ home, Eleanor received him in the sitting room where she had once told him to leave Daniel alone. The lakefront plans were no longer spread across the table. In their place lay a stack of campaign papers and the overdue bill.
Billy took off his plaid cap. Eleanor left her dark glasses on.
“Would you like tea?”
“After we’ve talked.”
She sat opposite him. “You gave Miss Jenkins that invoice.”
“Yes.”
“You might have come to me first.”

“I did come to you. About Daniel’s machine. You told me not to question him.” Billy opened his notebook. “Then I found you at the Defender. We talked, but you never answered my question about the call.”
Eleanor drew the invoice toward her. “And now you think this answers it.”
“It answers a different question. The landlord says you paid Daniel’s rent. Jenny says you told her you hadn’t.”
For a while, Eleanor studied the page. Outside, someone was sweeping the front path. Each scrape of the broom reached the quiet room.
“I paid some bills,” she said at last. “Daniel was having difficulty keeping his laboratory.”
“Then why tell Jenny no?”
“I wasn’t going to discuss a private arrangement with a reporter minutes before my announcement.”
“That isn’t what she asked.”
Eleanor put the invoice down. “You’ve always had a way of making Daniel sound worse than he is.”
Billy stopped his pencil above the paper. “His nephew tore a café roof loose. Daniel sent him there. Later, his robot overturned cars on Superior Avenue.”
“I saw the damage.”
“Did you know about the robot when you paid those bills?”
“No.” Her answer came quickly. “He told me he was working on the lake.”
Billy wrote down her words. Paying the rent did not prove she had known what stood in the workshop. Her answer did not prove she hadn’t.
“He asked for money for research,” Eleanor continued. “I thought Cleveland might benefit. Claude wanted people back at the waterfront. Daniel said he could help.”
“Did you ask for his results?”
“He showed me equipment.”
“That wasn’t what I asked.”
Her fingers tightened around the edge of the invoice. Billy waited, but she gave him no measurements, no dates, and no names of anyone who had checked Daniel’s work.
“Did you telephone Jenny’s editor?” he asked.
“I speak to newspaper editors, William. I’m running for mayor.”
“Before that. The call that got Daniel’s cleanup claim printed.”
Eleanor looked toward the window. “I won’t have every conversation I’ve ever had turned into an accusation.”
Billy left a line beneath the question. “And the police? Who told them to hold back?”
“You should ask their commanding officer.”
“I intend to.” He looked up. “I’m asking whether you spoke to anyone about Daniel.”
She stood and gathered the campaign papers into a neat pile. “We’re finished for this morning.”
Billy closed his notebook, keeping one finger between the pages. “Where is he?”
“I don’t know.”
“Has he contacted you since the robot fell?”
Eleanor gathered the campaign papers against her chest. “Daniel told me you’ve been working with the Defenders of the Land.”
Billy opened his notebook again. “When did he tell you that?”
“That boy. The glove. Going into laboratories, wrecking equipment. You’re supposed to know better, William.”
“When did you hear from him?”

“Stop skipping around the city with them. Stay out of Daniel’s affairs.” She set the papers down hard enough to shift the invoice. “When I’m mayor, I’ll put your vigilantes in jail if you keep this up.”
blocks.alt: In the Blackwells’ sitting room in 1987, silver-haired Eleanor wears dark glasses and points at Billy while threatening his vigilante friends. Billy, short and stocky in his high-collared trench coat, holds an open notebook; his plaid cap, an overdue laboratory invoice and campaign papers lie on the table.

blocks.text: Billy kept his pencil still. “For stopping his robot?”
“For taking the law into their own hands. You don’t get to decide whose property they can destroy.”
“And Daniel doesn’t get to decide whose car he can overturn.” Billy looked at her over the notebook. “You’ve heard from the man the police need to question. Have you told them?”
“He didn’t tell me where he was.”
“Did you ask?”
Eleanor reached for the invoice instead of answering.
“Tell the police he contacted you,” Billy said. “Let them ask him about Superior Avenue. My friends saved people there.”
“I’m trying to keep you out of trouble.”
Billy put on his cap. “Then help me find Daniel. Don’t threaten the people who stopped him.”
She held out the invoice. “Take this back to the landlord. Tell him I’ll settle the overdue amount. After that, Daniel must make his own arrangements.”
Billy accepted the page. “Jenny will need your answer too. She gave your office a chance to explain.”
“I’ll speak to my office.”
At the door, Eleanor caught his sleeve. For a moment, she looked as though she might say something else. Then she straightened the fold in his coat.
“You used to visit without that notebook.”
Billy looked down at her hand. “You used to ask how I was.”
She let him go.

Back at his desk, he telephoned Jenny. He told her about the rent, then read her Eleanor’s threat. “Daniel has contacted her,” he said. “She wouldn’t say when. She knows I’m working with the Defenders, but she didn’t name you.” Jenny asked him to read the exact words twice.
“I’ll ask her office to confirm,” she said. “And I’ll check the payment history with the landlord.”
Billy opened his notebook to the blank line beneath the question about the editor’s call. Below it, he wrote the police commanding officer’s name from his earlier notes.

Eleanor had admitted paying the rent. Now he knew she had heard from Daniel, too. Billy wrote down the threat beneath her answers. She wanted him to stop asking questions. He turned to a clean page and began listing the ones he still needed answered.
